title: Where does God live?
hook: the Kotzker Rebbe answers his students: wherever people let God in (Hasidic tale)
tomorrow: the north wind and the sun

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaac walked to Prague and found his otzar at home. Your line was it was under the stove. What good thing did you find close by? Day sixty-three, the last day of the Jewish wisdom week.

Kids ask the best questions. Where was I before I was born? Why is the sky that color? And, sooner or later, if God is real, where does God live? Adults tend to answer fast, and a little embarrassed: everywhere, sweetie. Today's story is about a rabbi who asked that exact question to a room full of adults, and wasn't satisfied with the fast answer. He was Menachem Mendel of Kotzk, known as the Kotzker Rebbe, a Hasidic master in Poland, remembered as fierce, brilliant and allergic to anything fake. One day, the tale goes, he turns to some learned visitors and asks: where does God live? Today's story is where does God live?
screen: `KIDS ASK THE BEST QUESTIONS.` → `THE KOTZKER REBBE.` → `WHERE DOES GOD LIVE?`

segments.voice: The visitors laugh. What a question, Rebbe! Everyone knows the answer. The prophet Isaiah says it. In his vision, the seraphim call out, in the King James words: "the whole earth is full of his glory." God is everywhere. And the Kotzker shakes his head. No, he says. God lives wherever people let God in. It's a small sentence that changes the whole picture. The visitors gave the textbook answer, and it's true in their tradition: God fills the world. But the rebbe is asking something else. Not where God is, in theory, but where God is actually at home: where a presence is welcomed, noticed, given room. A house can be full of air and still feel shut. The Hebrew tradition has a word for God's indwelling presence, Shekhinah, from a root that means to dwell, to live somewhere. The Kotzker's point is that the dwelling isn't only up to God. It's also a door that people open, or keep closed. For listeners who don't use the word God, the story still speaks. Whatever you call what's sacred, awe, love, presence, it tends to live where it's let in. Now look back at this week. zil g'mor. haruv. Zusya's question. Two pockets. The whistle. The treasure under the stove. And now, where does God live. Seven tales from Jewish tradition, and nearly every one turns on something small and close: one line, one tree, one self, one note, one whistle, one stove, one open door.
screen: `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL OF HIS GLORY.` · `WHEREVER PEOPLE LET GOD IN.` · `SHEKHINAH: THE INDWELLING.` · `SEVEN TALES, SMALL AND CLOSE.` · then, large: `LET IT IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a door and pause in it. If you can, stand up and go to a door, any door, and open it. Stand in the doorway. If you can't move right now, picture one. Feel the air change. Notice the threshold under your feet. If you pray, you can let God in, in your own way. If you don't, let in whatever is sacred to you: stillness, gratitude, the day itself. Just stand in the open door, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Shekhinah, God's indwelling presence. The Kotzker Rebbe's answer to where God lives: wherever people let God in.
Your line: let it in. Today, each time you walk through a doorway, pause for one breath and open something inside too. That closes the Jewish wisdom week. Day sixty-three.

howItsDone: The Kotzker's saying is quoted in Jewish teaching and sermons, and Jewish homes traditionally have a mezuzah on the doorposts, which some people touch on the way in and out as a reminder of God's presence.
